headline_marked: Privacy-First AI: [[Fine-Tuning Llama-3 on Your MacBook to Decipher 10 Years of Health Reports]]
headline: Privacy-First AI: Fine-Tuning Llama-3 on Your MacBook to Decipher 10 Years of Health Reports
summary: Leverage Apple Silicon and the MLX framework to fine-tune Meta's Llama-3 locally on your MacBook, transforming a decade of personal health data into actionable insights without compromising privacy.
details: In an era where personal data, especially medical history, is highly sensitive, the idea of uploading ten years of health reports to a cloud provider raises significant privacy concerns. This guide addresses that by enabling a private, medical-grade AI assistant to run entirely on your local machine.

By leveraging Apple Silicon optimization and the MLX framework, it's now possible to fine-tune Meta's Llama-3 model to understand personal health longitudinal data. This approach ensures that not a single byte of sensitive information leaves your hardware.

The process involves using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), which freezes the original model weights and trains only a small "adapter" layer. This technique makes it feasible to fine-tune a massive model like Llama-3 on a consumer laptop, bypassing traditional VRAM bottlenecks.

Apple’s Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) is crucial, allowing the GPU to access the entire system RAM. This means if your MacBook has 64GB of RAM, your LLM effectively has 64GB of "VRAM," providing ample resources for complex local AI tasks.

To fine-tune effectively, 10 years of PDF health reports are transformed into a structured dataset.jsonl. Each entry represents a medical context and a corresponding analysis, teaching the model to recognize trends in specific biomarkers over time.

Once training is complete, the model can run inference using the new adapters, remembering your historical data context without needing repeated prompting. For example, it can analyze vitamin D levels over years and suggest discussing supplementation with a doctor based on trends.

headline_marked: Report: [[AI e-waste could fill 23 million shipping containers by 2050]], circling the world 6 times
headline: Report: AI e-waste could fill 23 million shipping containers by 2050, circling the world 6 times
summary: A new report vastly underestimates previous figures, revealing AI's e-waste could reach 395 to 617 million metric tons by mid-century, posing a 'cataclysmic toxic waste crisis'.
details: A new report warns that e-waste from the AI boom has been vastly underestimated, projecting it could amount to 395 to 617 million metric tons by 2050. This staggering volume is enough trash to fill 23 million shipping containers, which could circle the world six times if lined up.

This significantly higher estimate, published by the nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN), factors in all the infrastructure needed to support servers in data centers. Previous studies focused primarily on servers and GPUs, missing about 87 percent of a data center's electro-mechanical infrastructure.

Jim Puckett, founder of BAN, stated that AI, despite feeling weightless, relies on enormous amounts of specialized hardware. He emphasized the urgent need for companies and governments to plan for this 'new waste tsunami' to prevent an even more severe toxic waste crisis.

Globally, less than a quarter of the 68.3 million tons of e-waste generated annually is formally collected and recycled. Most ends up in informal waste collection, where burning or burying equipment exposes workers and the environment to toxic materials like lead and chromium.

The US, which hosts more data centers than any other country, has not ratified the Basel Convention, designed to limit the international trade of hazardous wastes. Investigations show US recyclers still ship e-waste abroad, often leading to 'backyard recycling' that threatens the health of millions of children.

BAN predicts global e-waste will triple to 211 million metric tons per year by 2050, with AI contributing 15 to 20 percent. Their expanded count includes power supply, cooling systems, backup power, networking equipment, and 'AI Waste Contagion' — devices made obsolete by AI advances.

The report calculates 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. Citing a McKinsey projection of total data center capacity reaching up to 219GW by 2030, BAN's figures account for AI-related electronic equipment retired between 2025 and 2050.

Previous estimates for AI e-waste were more conservative, with one 2024 study predicting 1.2 million to 5 million tons by 2030. Another study in February found AI servers could create 131,000 to 225,000 tons annually by the decade's end, comparable to Denmark's total e-waste.
